# Transforming time series

## Variance stabilisation

If the data show different variation at different levels of the series, then a transformation can be useful.

::: {.fragment}
Denote original observations as $y_1,\dots,y_n$ and transformed
observations as $w_1, \dots, w_n$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## Mathematical transformations for stabilising variation

$$\begin{array}{llc}
\text{Square root} & w_t = \sqrt{y_t} & \downarrow \\
\text{Cube root} & w_t = \sqrt[3]{y_t} & \text{Increasing} \\
\text{Logarithm} & w_t = \text{log}(y_t) & \text{strength}
\end{array}$$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Logarithms, in particular, are useful because they are more interpretable: changes in a log value are **relative (percent) changes on the original scale**.
:::

## Variance stabilisation

```{r food, echo=TRUE}
food <- aus_retail |>
  filter(Industry == "Food retailing") |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover))
```

```{r food-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height=3.8}
food |> autoplot(Turnover) +
  labs(y = "Turnover ($AUD)")
```

## Variance stabilisation

```{r food-sqrt1, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3.8}
food |> autoplot(sqrt(Turnover)) +
  labs(y = "Square root turnover")
```

## Variance stabilisation

```{r food-cbrt, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3.8}
food |> autoplot(Turnover^(1 / 3)) +
  labs(y = "Cube root turnover")
```

## Variance stabilisation

```{r food-log, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3.8}
food |> autoplot(log(Turnover)) +
  labs(y = "Log turnover")
```

## Variance stabilisation

```{r food-inverse, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3.8}
food |> autoplot(-1 / Turnover) +
  labs(y = "Negative inverse turnover")
```

Which transformation best stabilises the variance of food turnover?

- Square root

:::

## Box-Cox transformations

Each of these transformations is close to a member of the
family of **Box-Cox transformations**:
$$w_t = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
        \text{log}(y_t),      & \quad \lambda = 0; \\
        (\text{sign}(y_t)|y_t|^\lambda-1)/\lambda ,         & \quad \lambda \ne 0.
\end{array}\right.
$$

::: {.fragment}
* Actually the Bickel-Doksum transformation (allowing for $y_t<0$)
* $\lambda=1$: (No substantive transformation)
* $\lambda=\frac12$: (Square root plus linear transformation)
* $\lambda=0$: (Natural logarithm)
* $\lambda=-1$: (Negative inverse plus 1)
:::

## Box-Cox transformations

```{r}
#| label: food-boxcox
#| echo: false
webr_slider(
  food, x = "Month",
  fn = function(data, lambda) {
    y <- data$Turnover
    data.frame(Turnover = if (lambda == 0) log(y) else (sign(y) * abs(y)^lambda - 1) / lambda)
  },
  sliders = list(
    lambda = list(
      label = "λ", value = 1, min = -1, max = 2, step = 0.01,
      ticks = seq(-1, 2, by = 0.5)
    )
  ),
  title = "Box-Cox transformed food retailing turnover (λ = {lambda})",
  height = 475
)
```

## Box-Cox transformations

::: {.likert #boxcox-lambda labels="0–0.1|0.1–0.2|0.2–0.3|0.3–0.4|0.4–0.5|0.5–0.6|0.6–0.7|0.7–0.8|0.8–0.9|0.9–1.0"}
What is the best value of λ for food retailing turnover?
:::

## Box-Cox transformations


```{r food-lambda, echo=TRUE}
food |>
  features(Turnover, features = guerrero)
```

::: {.fragment}
* This attempts to balance the seasonal fluctuations and random variation across the series.
* Always check the results.
* A low value of $\lambda$ can give extremely large prediction intervals.
:::

## Box-Cox transformations

```{r food-bc, echo=TRUE,fig.height=3.8}
food |> autoplot(box_cox(Turnover, 0.0895)) +
  labs(y = "Box-Cox transformed turnover")
```

## Transformations

* Often no transformation needed.
* Simple transformations are easier to explain and work well enough.
* Transformations can have very large effect on PI.
* If some data are zero or negative, then use $\lambda>0$.
* `log1p()` can also be useful for data with zeros.
* Choosing logs is a simple way to force forecasts to be positive
* Transformations must be reversed to obtain forecasts on the original scale. (Handled automatically by `fable`.)

## Per capita adjustments

```{r gdp-per-capita}
global_economy |>
  filter(Country == "Australia") |>
  autoplot(GDP)
```

## Inflation adjustments {.code-small}

```{r, eval=FALSE}
print_retail <- aus_retail |>
  filter(Industry == "Newspaper and book retailing") |>
  group_by(Industry) |>
  index_by(Year = year(Month)) |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover))
aus_economy <- filter(global_economy, Country == "Australia")
print_retail |>
  left_join(aus_economy, by = "Year") |>
  mutate(Adj_turnover = Turnover / CPI) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Turnover, Adj_turnover),
    names_to = "Type", values_to = "Turnover"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = Turnover)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(vars(Type), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Years", y = NULL,
       title = "Turnover: Australian print media industry")
```

## Inflation adjustments

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, out.width="80%"}
print_retail <- aus_retail |>
  filter(Industry == "Newspaper and book retailing") |>
  group_by(Industry) |>
  index_by(Year = year(Month)) |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover))
aus_economy <- filter(tsibbledata::global_economy, Country == "Australia")
print_retail |>
  left_join(aus_economy, by = "Year") |>
  mutate(Adj_turnover = Turnover / CPI) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Turnover, Adj_turnover),
    names_to = "Type", values_to = "Turnover"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = Turnover)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(vars(Type), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Years", y = NULL,
    title = "Turnover: Australian print media industry"
  )
```


# Time series decompositions

## Time series decomposition

Trend-Cycle
: aperiodic changes in level over time.

Seasonal
: (almost) periodic changes in level due to seasonal factors (e.g., the quarter of the year, the month, or day of the week).

::: {.callout-note}
## Additive decomposition

$$ y_t = S_t + T_t + R_t $$
:::

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{where}\quad & y_t = \text{ data at period } t \\
& T_t = \text{ trend-cycle component at period } t \\
& S_t = \text{ seasonal component at period } t \\
& R_t = \text{ remainder component at period } t
\end{aligned}$$

## STL decomposition


  *  STL: "Seasonal and Trend decomposition using Loess"
  *  Very versatile and robust.
  *  Seasonal component allowed to change over time, and rate of change controlled by user.
  *  Smoothness of trend-cycle also controlled by user.
  *  Optionally robust to outliers
  *  No trading day or calendar adjustments.
  *  Only additive.
  *  Take logs to get multiplicative decomposition.
  *  Use Box-Cox transformations to get other decompositions.

## Seasonal adjustment

  *  Useful by-product of decomposition:  an easy way to calculate seasonally adjusted data.
  *  Additive decomposition: seasonally adjusted data given by
$$y_t - S_t = T_t + R_t$$
  *  Multiplicative decomposition: seasonally adjusted data given by
$$y_t / S_t = T_t \times R_t$$

## US Retail Employment

```{r usretail-sa, fig.height=2.7}
us_retail_employment |>
  autoplot(Employed, color = "gray") +
  autolayer(components(dcmp), season_adjust, color = "#0072B2") +
  labs(y = "Persons (thousands)", title = "Total employment in US retail")
```

## Seasonal adjustment

  * We use estimates of $S$ based on past values to seasonally adjust a current value.
  *  Seasonally adjusted series reflect **remainders** as well as **trend**. Therefore they are not "smooth" and "downturns" or "upturns" can be misleading.
  *  It is better to use the trend-cycle component to look for turning points.

## STL decomposition

```{r}
#| label: stl-window
#| echo: false
# Trend windows up to the length of the data, then up to the smallest window
# whose fit is exactly linear: stl() fits the trend every ceiling(t.window/10)
# points and interpolates, so it fits only the two ends from 10 * (n - 2) + 1
n <- nrow(us_retail_employment)
webr_slider(
  us_retail_employment |> select(Month, Employed), x = "Month",
  fn = function(data, s_window, t_window) {
    fit <- stl(ts(data$Employed, frequency = 12),
      s.window = s_window, t.window = t_window, robust = TRUE
    )$time.series
    data.frame(
      Employed = data$Employed, trend = fit[, "trend"],
      season_year = fit[, "seasonal"], remainder = fit[, "remainder"]
    )
  },
  sliders = list(
    t_window = list(
      label = "Trend window", value = 21, min = 7,
      max = 10 * (n - 2) + 1, step = 2, log = TRUE,
      ticks = c(7, 13, 25, 51, 101, n, 1001, 10 * (n - 2) + 1)
    ),
    s_window = list(
      label = "Seasonal window", value = 13, min = 5, max = 55, step = 2,
      log = TRUE, ticks = c(5, 7, 9, 13, 19, 27, 39, 55)
    )
  ),
  title = "STL decomposition of US retail employment",
  subtitle = "trend(window = {t_window}) + season(window = {s_window})", height = 490
)
```


## STL decomposition

```{r echo = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
us_retail_employment |>
  model(STL(Employed ~ trend(window = 15) + season(window = "periodic"),
    robust = TRUE
  )) |>
  components()
```


  *  `trend(window = ?)` controls wiggliness of trend component.
  *  `season(window = ?)` controls variation on seasonal component.
  *  `season(window = 'periodic')` is equivalent to an infinite window.

## STL decomposition

```{r mstl, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=3.4}
us_retail_employment |>
  model(STL(Employed)) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot()
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.alertblock .absolute top="0px" right="0px" width="500px" style="font-size:0.7em;"}
* `STL()` chooses `season(window=13)` by default
* Can include transformations.
:::
:::

## STL decomposition

* Algorithm that updates trend and seasonal components iteratively.
* Starts with $\hat{T}_t=0$
* Uses a mixture of loess and moving averages to successively refine the trend and seasonal estimates.
* trend window controls loess bandwidth on deseasonalised values.
* season window controls loess bandwidth on detrended subseries.
* Robustness weights based on remainder.
* Default season: `window = 13`
* Default trend: `window = nextodd(ceiling((1.5*period)/(1-(1.5/s.window))))`
* `window` values should be odd numbers for symmetry.

# STL Features

## Strength of seasonality and trend

::: {.callout-important}
## STL decomposition

::: {.center-text}
$y_t = T_t+S_t+R_t$
:::
:::

### Seasonal strength
$$\max\left(0, 1-\frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t+R_t)}\right)$$

### Trend strength
$$\max\left(0, 1-\frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(T_t+R_t)}\right)$$

Both range from 0 (none) to 1 (strong), computed by `feat_stl()`.

## STL features {.code-small}

`tourism`: quarterly overnight trips (thousands) for 304 Australian domestic series, keyed by Region, State and Purpose.

```{r features}
tourism |> features(Trips, feat_stl)
```

## STL features

* `trend_strength`, `seasonal_strength_year`: strength of the trend and seasonal components.
* `seasonal_peak_year`, `seasonal_trough_year`: the quarter with the largest and smallest seasonal component.
* `spikiness`: prevalence of spikes in the remainder.
* `linearity`, `curvature`: shape of the trend, from a quadratic regression on time.
* `stl_e_acf1`: first autocorrelation of the remainder.
* `stl_e_acf10`: sum of squares of the first ten autocorrelations of the remainder.

## Seasonal and trend strength {.code-tiny}

```{r}
#| label: features-plot
#| fig-height: 3.6
tourism |>
  features(Trips, feat_stl) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trend_strength, y = seasonal_strength_year, col = Purpose)) +
  geom_point() + facet_wrap(vars(State)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1))
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.alertblock .absolute top="530px" left="860px" width="340px" style="font-size:0.7em;"}
* Holidays more seasonal than other travel.
* WA series tend to have the strongest trends.
:::
:::

## Most seasonal and most trended series {.code-small}

```{r extremes}
stl_features <- tourism |> features(Trips, feat_stl)
extremes <- bind_rows(
  "Most seasonal" = slice_max(stl_features, seasonal_strength_year),
  "Most trended" = slice_max(stl_features, trend_strength),
  .id = "Feature"
)
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r extremes-plot, fig.height=2.1}
tourism |>
  inner_join(extremes, by = join_by(State, Region, Purpose)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Quarter, y = Trips)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(vars(Feature, State, Region, Purpose), scales = "free_y",
    labeller = labeller(.multi_line = FALSE))
```
:::

## ACF features {.code-small}

```{r featuresacf}
tourism |> features(Trips, feat_acf)
```

## ACF features

* `acf1`: first autocorrelation of the series.
* `acf10`: sum of squares of the first ten autocorrelations.
* `diff1_acf1`, `diff1_acf10`: the same, for the differenced series.
* `diff2_acf1`, `diff2_acf10`: the same, for the twice differenced series.
* `season_acf1`: autocorrelation at the first seasonal lag.

# Clustering features

## All feasts features {.code-tiny}

All features from the feasts package:

```{r tourismfeatures}
tourism_features <- tourism |>
  features(Trips, feature_set(pkgs = "feasts"))
tourism_features
```

## Principal components {.code-tiny}

Principal components are combinations of the 48 features with the most variation, so the 304 series can be compared in two dimensions:

```{r pcatable}
pcs <- tourism_features |>
  select(-State, -Region, -Purpose) |>
  prcomp(scale. = TRUE) |>
  broom::augment(tourism_features)
pcs |> select(Region, State, Purpose, .fittedPC1, .fittedPC2)
```

## PC1 vs PC2 {.code-small}

```{r pca1-plot}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "85%"
pcs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## PCs coloured by State {.code-small}

```{r pca2-plot}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "85%"
pcs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2,
             col = State)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## PCs coloured by Purpose {.code-small}

Holiday series sit higher on both PCs than other travel purposes.

```{r pca3-plot}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "85%"
pcs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2,
             col = Purpose)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## Outliers in PC space {.code-small}

Four outlying series: PC1 > 12, or PC1 > 10 and PC2 > 0.

```{r pca-outliers}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "85%"
outliers <- pcs |>
  filter(.fittedPC1 > 12 |
           (.fittedPC1 > 10 & .fittedPC2 > 0))
pcs |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fittedPC1, y = .fittedPC2,
             col = Purpose)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = outliers, col = "black",
             shape = 1, size = 3) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## Outlying series

```{r outliers2, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=12}
tourism |>
  semi_join(outliers, by = join_by(State, Region, Purpose)) |>
  mutate(Series = glue("{State}", "{Region}", "{Purpose}", .sep = "\n\n")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Quarter, y = Trips)) +
  geom_line() + facet_grid(Series ~ .) +
  labs(title = "Outlying time series in PC space")
```
